# Agent Code

Agent Code is an agent-first editor for heavy users of Claude Code and Codex.

This is not another "make Claude Code look nicer" wrapper. It is an
agentic development platform built on the opposite assumption: the agent
runtime is the product. The UI exists to make Claude Code and Codex more
powerful, not to replace them with a thin chat shell and a coat of glass.

## Why This Exists

A lot of people are building their own UI for Claude Code right now. Most
of them hit the same two failure modes:

1. They optimize for surface aesthetics instead of agent capability.
2. They bypass the real product by driving unofficial or reduced flows that
   throw away the logic Claude Code and Codex already have.

That leads to tools that look polished but are materially weaker.

Agent Code takes a harder line:

- Claude Code should still feel like Claude Code.
- Codex should still feel like Codex.
- The full command surface, prompts, tools, flows, and runtime behavior
  should still exist.
- The UI should add power for serious users, not abstract away the thing
  that already works.

## Core Thesis

The best agent editor is not a fake Claude Code UI.

The best agent editor is a platform that runs the real Claude Code and the
real Codex under the hood, preserves their behavior, and then layers better
workspace primitives on top for people who spend all day in agent loops.

That means Agent Code is built for:

- parallel agent work
- persistent sessions
- richer workspace orchestration
- multi-pane and multi-provider flows
- better tooling around transcripts, state, terminals, and code context

## Not OAuth Token Abuse

Many wrappers depend on reusing OAuth tokens from Claude or Codex and then
calling private or reduced interfaces around the actual product.

That approach is bad on two fronts:

- It cuts against platform policy.
- It throws away an enormous amount of product logic that already exists in
  Claude Code and Codex.

If you strip things down to "send message, get message back", you lose most
of what makes those tools good in practice.

Agent Code is explicitly trying not to do that.

## How It Works

Agent Code runs Claude Code and Codex headlessly under the hood.

But "headless" here does **not** mean using a minimal session API and
pretending that is the product.

It means using open source headless runtimes that emulate the actual CLI and
terminal behavior of Claude Code and Codex so the shell can expose the full
system programmatically.

The architecture combines:

- terminal emulation
- JSON/event parsing
- screen parsing
- transcript parsing
- session management

This lets Agent Code surface the real commands, flows, and tools from Claude
Code and Codex in an API-like way without collapsing them into a toy chat
interface.

In practice, the stack includes:

- `claude-code-headless`: headless control layer for Claude Code
- `codex-headless`: headless control layer for Codex
- `agent-transcript-parser`: translation layer between transcript formats
- Electron + React workspace shell on top

## What This Project Is

Agent Code is:

- an Electron desktop shell for agent-heavy development
- a multi-session workspace for Claude Code, Codex, and terminals
- a way to preserve nearly all of the real agent behavior while adding a
  stronger editor and workspace model around it

It is not:

- a "Claude Code but prettier" theme project
- a thin chat app with editor chrome
- a wrapper that replaces the underlying product with a reduced API

## Philosophy

The job is not to "macify" Claude Code.

The job is to build the editor serious agent users actually need:

- keep the underlying agents real
- preserve the capabilities that already exist
- expose more control, more observability, and more workspace power
- build for people who live in long-running, high-volume agent sessions

If the result ever looks nicer, that is incidental. Capability comes first.

## Status

This repository is an active build. The current app already contains the
foundation for:

- Claude Code sessions
- Codex sessions
- plain terminal sessions
- tabbed and tiled workspace UI
- provider-aware session handling
- transcript and runtime parsing
- local desktop hosting through Electron

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Build:

```bash
npm run build
```

This is a duplicate of the post on juliusolsson.com/agent-code.

Agent Code is an open-source Electron-based AI-native IDE built by me. This post is about showcasing it.

## Why build this?

OpenCode is amazing. Cursor is amazing. The issue with these is that their software models are facing a hard time. Because of one reason:

OAuth is being killed.

You can no longer use Anthropic models properly in OpenCode, and Cursor's pricing is getting more brutal by the day if you do not lock yourself into their internal models.

But everybody wants to use SOTA models, which basically means Claude's latest and Codex's latest releases. Codex is liberal with OAuth usage as of me writing this, but my prediction is that that will not last forever. This is history repeating itself; in the 2010s the definition of the internet was "open." Everybody had free APIs to access their whole software suite. Facebook, Google, Yahoo, etc. This just slowly got killed by the companies. The difference is that, as with everything in AI, it is compressing the internet's timeline into 5 years instead of 20, and we already saw Anthropic banning OAuth.

## What Agent Code does differently

Instead of trying to go around Claude Code and Codex, it is just the middleman. When you use the app, a headless CLI for Claude and Codex is spawned. Do not confuse this with the SDK that is natively exposed, because that is limited and drops 75% of the functionality that lives in Codex and Claude. What Agent Code runs in a PTY is the FULL native Claude Code and Codex. This allows us to keep and maintain all new and custom functionality that these providers expose.

## So why do this?

Building an app like this lets me add any abstractions that I want, but the main motivations behind it were the following:

**1. Provider switching.**
I built a package that Agent Code calls for this sole purpose: [agent-transcript-parser](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-transcript-parser). This allows you to have a Codex session open, open the command palette and switch to Claude in one click, by natively translating the JSONL transcript between the two providers.

**2. Heavy development focus.**
This might be the most important part. Codex and Claude's apps focus on having one session on the screen and feel like they are built for lightweight agent development. Using agents properly requires having 5 running at all times. Agent Code gives you excellent tiling built in to manage all of your agents in a grid structure.

**3. Custom rendering.**
Because we are positioning Agent Code as a middleman, we rewrite all the rendering in React. This allows us to do whatever we want. For example, we built a better UI to see what the agents committed and ran for git commands.

**4. Opinionated for efficiency.**
The whole app is built for efficient development. All terminals are tmux-persistent by default alongside all agents. There are 50+ commands which are all excellent to boost productivity on top of the agents.

## Structure

One of the principles I understood early is that getting open-source contributors on board with something like this is hard. So Agent Code is dependent on 4 separate projects that it imports as packages, all more broadly scoped, which will hopefully attract more open-source attention.

## Structure

One of the principles I understood early is that getting open-source contributors on board with something like this is hard. So Agent Code is dependent on 4 separate projects that it imports as packages — all more broadly scoped, which will hopefully attract more open-source attention.

**1. Headless Claude Code and Codex**
[claude-code-headless](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/claude-code-headless) · [codex-headless](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/codex-headless)
This is basically the core of the app. It takes the full Claude CLI and Codex CLI and exposes them as an API, so that you can control all actions that you would be able to do in the CLI programmatically instead. For example, detecting the state when the agent is running a compaction or when the agent is asking for folder permission. You could take this and make it the backend of any project you want.

**2. [Agent Transcript Parser](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-transcript-parser)**
As mentioned before — takes a JSONL transcript from Codex and converts it to Claude or vice versa with complete roundtrip safety.

**3. [Agent Voice Dictation](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-voice-dictation)**

Worth mentioning that Agent Code is opinionated with cleverness over the whole suite. For instance: WhisprFlow is stupid — they are trying to correct spelling mistakes on the wrong level. <stt note="Speech-to-text; may contain transcription mistakes.">
```xml
Now I am speaking.
</stt>
```

# Agent Code

This codebase is written and developed by AI. Future you will pick up where past you left off, with no shared memory beyond what's in the repo.

## Comment policy

Write **thick WHY comments** liberally throughout the code. Be generous — over-comment, don't under-comment. The cost of an extra paragraph is nothing; the cost of future-you re-deriving a tricky decision from scratch is real.

A good comment answers questions like:

- *Why this approach and not the obvious alternative?*
- *What constraint forced this shape?*
- *What did we try first that didn't work?*
- *What invariant must hold here, and what breaks if it doesn't?*
- *What's the source of truth for this value?*

Don't bother explaining *what* the code does — that's what reading the code is for. Explain *why it exists*, *why it's shaped this way*, and *what would make it wrong*.

Make agentic development and decision-making **transparent in the diff**, not in a doc that drifts.

# Reporting Issues

This codebase is worked on primarily by AI agents. This guide is for
them.

**The more technical detail, the better.** File paths with line numbers,
exact symbols, transcript IDs, commit SHAs, error output verbatim,
stack traces, environment variables — over-share rather than
under-share. Every fact you omit is a follow-up round trip the next
person has to do before they can reproduce.

## Which repo

| Repo | What goes here |
|---|---|
| **agent-code** | UI, tile-tree, dispatch, session management, IPC, system-perf, settings — all renderer + main-process behaviour. Default. |
| **claude-code-headless** | Driving the real `claude` CLI: TUI parsing, JSONL handling, proxy/SSE streaming, slash-picker, permission prompts. |
| **codex-headless** | Driving the real `codex` CLI: rollout parsing, Responses adapter, screen parsing, approval overlays. |
| **agent-transcript-parser** | Claude↔Codex transcript translation, ghost primitives, rewind/clone helpers. |
| **agent-voice-dictation** | Recording, STT clients, OpenRouter polish, composer integration. |

## Bug report

```markdown
### What happened
One or two sentences. The visible symptom.

### Repro
Exact steps. If non-deterministic, say so explicitly and describe how
often / under what conditions: "happens after ~30 min of normal use
with 10+ agents active." Link the relevant transcript path —
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-foo-bar/<sessionId>.jsonl` for Claude or
`~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<timestamp>-<id>.jsonl` for
Codex. Include the commit SHA you reproduced on.

### Where
File:line and the function or symbol if you've located it. Examples:
`src/main/sessionManager.ts:912 spawnClaude`,
`src/renderer/src/features/feed/ui/Feed.tsx onScroll`,
`packages/claude-code-headless/src/proxy/ClaudeProxyAdapter.ts:804`.
If unlocated, name the subsystem: feed renderer, JSONL tailer, proxy
adapter, dispatch mode, work-context, image paste, dictation.

### Output
Error text, stack trace, log lines — verbatim, don't paraphrase or
truncate. Include surrounding console lines if a single line was the
trigger but the context is in the lines around it. Native frames
(C++/Rust) in a v8 fatal-error trace are important — keep them.

### State
Anything that affects reproducibility: number of active panes, which
providers (Claude / Codex / terminal), how long the app had been
running, whether `AGENT_CODE_PERF` was set, whether you were in
Dispatch Mode, whether worktrees were attached.
```

## Feature request

```markdown
### Use case
The workflow the current app makes harder than it should be.

### Example
One concrete scenario, end to end — what you'd do today vs. what you
wish you could do.

### (Optional) Sketch
Implementation thoughts. Skip unless you have specifics.
```

## Performance / crash

Different evidence than functional bugs. Attach what applies:

- **Fatal-error block from the terminal.** When the main process
  OOM's, the terminal where `npm start` ran will have a `FATAL
  ERROR: CALL_AND_RETRY_LAST Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out
  of memory` line followed by a `Native stack trace` block. Include
  the whole block, not just the headline — the native frames identify
  the allocator that broke (typical signatures: `node::Buffer::New`,
  `v8::CppHeap::wrapper_descriptor`, Rust `font_types::...`).
- **System-perf popover state at the time.** Requires
  `AGENT_CODE_PERF=1` set when launching. Click the heap badge in the
  header. Report: heap used / limit, RSS, top heap spaces with sizes
  (especially `old_space` and `large_object_space`),
  detached-contexts count, native-contexts count, event-loop p99,
  60s growth Δ for heap and RSS.
- **Heap snapshot.** Manual: click "Capture heap snapshot" in the
  popover; writes to `~/.config/agent-code/heap-snapshots/manual-<iso>-<pid>.heapsnapshot`.
  Automatic: the watchdog writes one when `used_heap_size` crosses
  `min(3 GiB, 0.75 × heap_size_limit)` — same directory, `main-` prefix.
  These files are 10–500 MB; link a cloud share rather than attaching
  directly if large.
- **Growth pattern.** Three shapes matter:
  - steady monotonic climb → retention leak
  - spike-up-then-drop-to-zero cycle → transient large allocations
    (whole-file reads, big buffers, GC churn)
  - sudden jump → one-shot allocation (giant string, image, file load)

  Saying which shape you observed narrows the suspect list before
  anyone opens the snapshot.

## Security

Disclose privately to the maintainer rather than via a public GitHub
issue.

## Don't file

- How-to questions → Discussions.
- Upstream CLI bugs (`claude` / `codex` flag behaviour) → the upstream
  repos for those tools, not here.

I've now read through the project's core documentation, structure, and history. Here's the complete picture of what **Agent Code** is.

---

# Agent Code — what this project is

**Agent Code is an open-source, Electron-based, AI-native IDE** — an "agent-first editor" built for people who run Claude Code and Codex *all day, in parallel*. It's written and maintained almost entirely by AI agents (you), with the repo itself being the only shared memory between sessions.

It's your own project (juliusolsson.com/agent-code), currently at version `0.0.2-beta.1`.

## The core thesis

Most people building Claude Code UIs make one of two mistakes:
1. They optimize for **looks** instead of agent capability ("Claude Code but prettier").
2. They **bypass the real product** — driving the limited SDK or reusing OAuth tokens against private/reduced interfaces, which throws away ~75% of the functionality that lives in the real CLIs.

Agent Code takes the opposite stance: **the agent runtime is the product; the UI exists to make it more powerful.** It runs the *full, real* `claude` and `codex` CLIs headlessly inside PTYs — not the stripped-down SDK — so the entire command surface, prompts, tools, permission flows, and runtime behavior are preserved. Claude Code should still feel like Claude Code; Codex should still feel like Codex. If it ends up looking nicer, that's incidental — capability comes first.

## The strategic bet (from MANIFESTO.md)

The motivating insight: **OAuth is being killed.** You can no longer use Anthropic models properly in OpenCode, and Cursor's pricing punishes you for using SOTA external models. The prediction is that the "open API" era of AI tools will close fast (history rhyming with how Facebook/Google/Yahoo killed their open APIs in the 2010s, but compressed into ~5 years). So instead of going *around* Claude Code and Codex, Agent Code becomes **the middleman** that drives them natively.

## How it works architecturally

A headless CLI for Claude/Codex is spawned in a PTY and controlled programmatically. The stack combines terminal emulation, JSON/event parsing, screen parsing, transcript parsing, and session management — exposing the real CLIs in an API-like way. On top sits an **Electron + React workspace shell**.

It's deliberately split into **separately-scoped packages** (in `packages/`) — partly so each can attract its own open-source contributors:

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| **claude-code-headless** | Drives the real `claude` CLI — TUI parsing, JSONL handling, proxy/SSE streaming, slash-picker, permission prompts |
| **codex-headless** | Drives the real `codex` CLI — rollout parsing, Responses adapter, screen parsing, approval overlays |
| **opencode-headless** | (additional headless control layer) |
| **agent-transcript-parser** | Translates JSONL transcripts between Claude ↔ Codex with roundtrip safety — this is what powers **one-click provider switching** mid-session |
| **agent-voice-dictation** | Open-source WhisprFlow clone on Deepgram; ships voice dictation natively into the composer (wraps STT output in an `<stt>` tag so the *model* fixes transcription errors, not a dumb pre-pass) |

## The four differentiators

1. **Provider switching** — open a Codex session, hit the command palette, switch to Claude in one click via native transcript translation.
2. **Heavy-development focus** — the real CLIs feel built for *one* session on screen; serious use means 5+ agents running at once. Agent Code gives you tiling/grid layout to manage them.
3. **Custom rendering** — as the middleman, all rendering is rewritten in React (e.g. a better UI for what agents committed and which git commands they ran).
4. **Opinionated for efficiency** — all terminals and agents are **tmux-persistent by default**; 50+ productivity commands layered on top.

## Source layout (`src/`)

- **`src/main/`** — Electron main process: `sessions`, `orchestration` (multi-agent), `aiWorkspace`, `tmux`, `providerSwitch`, `dictation`, `caffeinate`, `worktreeActivity`, `performance`, `storage`, `ipc`
- **`src/renderer/`** — React workspace UI (feed, tiling, panes)
- **`src/providers/`** — `claude`, `codex`, `shared` adapters
- **`src/mcp/`** — MCP runtime support
- **`src/shared/`** — git, parsers, runtime, types, work-context, rendered-content

## Repo conventions worth knowing

- **`vendor/`** = read-only source references (`claude-code-src`, `codex-src`) for grepping upstream implementations — never built or shipped.
- **`third_party/`** = pinned *runtime artifacts* the packaged app ships (`mitmproxy`, `tmux`); binaries are never committed — a `manifest.json` (version + per-arch sha256 + URL) is the source of truth.
- **Thick WHY comments** are mandated — explain *why* code exists and what would make it wrong, not what it does. Decision-making lives in the diff, not in drifting docs.
- **Issues** are written by AI agents for AI agents — maximal technical detail (file:line, transcript paths, commit SHAs, verbatim errors).
- Testing recently moved to **Vitest** (commit #263), with unit / integration / renderer projects.

## Current state

Active build. Already working: Claude Code sessions, Codex sessions, plain terminals, tabbed + tiled workspace UI, provider-aware session handling, transcript/runtime parsing, and local desktop hosting via Electron. Recent commit activity is heavily focused on the **feed rendering rewrite** and **orchestration** (multi-agent context inheritance, handoff scanning) — there are active rewrite plans in `docs/rendering/` and `docs/codex-rewrite-render/`.

---

In one line: **Agent Code is an Electron IDE that wraps the *real* Claude Code and Codex CLIs (not their reduced SDKs) to give power users parallel, tiled, persistent, provider-switchable agent sessions — betting that owning the middleman layer is the durable position as OAuth/open-API access gets locked down.**

Want me to go deeper on any specific subsystem — the orchestration/multi-agent layer, the rendering rewrite that's currently in flight, or how provider switching actually works under the hood?

======================================================================
# Tiled Dispatch

## Summary

Add a `Tiled Dispatch` command that lets the user enter a tile count, up to 10, and opens a multi-lane Dispatch layout where several live agents can be viewed and controlled at the same time.

## Problem

Dispatch Mode is useful for managing many agents, but it currently behaves like a single command-center surface. That means the user can see the list of agents, pick one, and work with that agent, but they cannot easily keep multiple active agents visible side by side from the Dispatch workflow.

When coordinating several Claude/Codex agents, the user often wants both:

- A full Dispatch index with all worktrees, section titles, agent types, and full agent titles.
- Multiple live agent views on screen at once, each with a small local selector for switching that lane to another agent.

The existing single Dispatch surface makes that workflow too serial.

## Proposed Behavior

Add a command:

```text
Tiled Dispatch
```

When run, the command prompts the user for a number:

```text
How many dispatch tiles? 1-10
```

After the user enters `N`, Agent Code enters a tiled Dispatch layout:

```text
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ DISPATCH INDEX       │ AGENT VIEW 1                 │ MINI LIST  │ AGENT VIEW 2                 │ MINI LIST  │ AGENT VIEW 3                 │
│ full list            │ selected agent               │ compact    │ selected agent               │ compact    │ selected agent               │
│                      │                              │            │                              │            │                              │
│ Worktree: app        │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ ● Agent A  │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ ● Agent B  │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
│  Claude  Agent A  ◀  │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │ ● Agent B◀ │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │ ● Agent C◀ │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │
│  Codex   Agent B     │ │ composer / terminal      │ │ ● Agent C  │ │ composer / terminal      │ │ ● Agent D  │ │ composer / terminal      │ │
│  Claude  Agent C     │ │ live output              │ │ ● Agent D  │ │ live output              │ │ ● Agent E  │ │ live output              │ │
│                      │ │                          │ │            │ │                          │ │            │ │                          │ │
│ Worktree: issue-211  │ │ selected from index      │ │ no groups  │ │ selected from mini list  │ │ no groups  │ │ selected from mini list  │ │
│  Codex   Agent D     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │ no cwd     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │ no cwd     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │
│  Claude  Agent E     │                              │ no type    │                              │ no type    │                              │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
```

For `N` tiled lanes, the conceptual layout is:

```text
[full dispatch index] [agent view 1] [mini list 2] [agent view 2] ... [mini list N] [agent view N]
```

The first lane is special:

- It keeps the full Dispatch list UI.
- It shows full section titles.
- It shows worktree/project grouping.
- It shows agent type/provider labels.
- It acts as the global index for the whole tiled Dispatch layout.

Every later lane uses a compact local selector:

- It shows a minimal agent list.
- It omits repeated section titles.
- It omits repeated worktree labels.
- It omits repeated agent type/provider labels.
- It is only there to switch which agent is shown in that lane.

Each lane still has a real live agent view beside its list. This is not just multiple copies of the Dispatch list; the point is to make multiple agents visible and usable at the same time.

## Scroll and Selection Sync

When the user scrolls a compact mini list, the full Dispatch index on the far left should follow that scroll position enough to keep the same region of the agent list/context visible. The full index remains the source of truth for rich context: section titles, worktrees, provider labels, and full agent titles.

Selection highlighting is separate from scroll sync:

- The full index still highlights the agent selected in lane 1.
- A compact mini list highlights the agent selected for its own lane.
- Scrolling mini list 3 should move the full index to the same approximate list region, but it should not make the full index pretend that lane 3's agent is selected.
- This lets the user use the full left index as context while still seeing exactly which agent belongs to lane 1.

In other words:

```text
Lane 3 mini list scrolls
        │
        ▼
Full left index follows scroll/context
        │
        └── but selected highlight remains Agent 1 / lane 1
```

## UX Notes

- The default tile count should be conservative, probably `2` or the previous value if one exists.
- The max should be clamped to `10`.
- The layout needs horizontal overflow or responsive compression for high tile counts.
- The first/full Dispatch index should stay readable even when there are many lanes.
- Compact mini lists should be dense and stable, optimized for quick lane switching.
- The selected agent per lane should be independent.
- Switching one lane should not steal focus or selection from the other lanes.
- Scrolling a compact mini list should sync the full index's scroll context, while preserving the full index's own selected-agent highlight.

## Open Questions

- Should tiled Dispatch persist across app reloads, or should it be a transient Dispatch view mode?
- Should each lane remember its selected agent by session id across normal Dispatch exits/reentries?
- Should lane widths be resizable?
- Should the full index lane be pinned/sticky while the right-side lanes horizontally scroll?
- Should tile count changes preserve current lane selections where possible?

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `Tiled Dispatch` command exists.
- Running it prompts for a tile count from `1` to `10`.
- Entering a valid count opens a tiled Dispatch layout.
- The leftmost lane shows the full Dispatch index with section titles, worktree grouping, provider/agent type labels, and full titles.
- Each additional lane shows a compact mini list plus the actual selected agent view to its right.
- Each lane can select a different live agent.
- Scrolling a compact mini list scroll-syncs the full left Dispatch index to the same general list region.
- The full left Dispatch index continues to highlight lane 1's selected agent, even while its scroll position follows another lane's mini list.
- The same agent process/session is reused; switching tiled views must not respawn agents.
- Exiting tiled Dispatch returns the user to the normal workspace without killing agents.
- Invalid counts are rejected or clamped safely.

That's **issue #248 — "Tiled Dispatch"** (no labels, no comments yet). Here's what it's about.

## The problem it solves
Dispatch Mode today is a **single command-center surface**: you see the list of all your agents, pick *one*, and work with it. That's serial. When you're coordinating 5+ Claude/Codex agents, you want two things at once that the current design can't give you:

1. A **full index** of every agent (worktrees, section titles, provider labels, full titles).
2. **Several live agent views side-by-side**, each independently switchable.

## The proposed feature
A new command, **`Tiled Dispatch`**, that prompts: *"How many dispatch tiles? 1–10"*. Enter `N` and you get a multi-lane layout:

```
[full dispatch index] [agent view 1] [mini list 2] [agent view 2] … [mini list N] [agent view N]
```

- **Lane 1 is special** — it keeps the *full* Dispatch list: section titles, worktree/project grouping, provider/type labels. It's the global index for the whole layout.
- **Every later lane** gets a **compact mini-list** (no repeated section titles/worktrees/labels — just enough to switch that lane) plus its own **live agent view** beside it.
- Each lane shows a *different live agent*, and they're independent — switching one lane doesn't steal focus or selection from another.

## The clever bit — scroll vs. selection decoupling
This is the subtle design point. When you scroll a mini-list (say lane 3), the **full left index follows that scroll position** so you keep rich context for the region you're browsing — **but the left index's *highlight* stays on lane 1's selected agent.** So scrolling lane 3 moves the index's viewport without making it pretend lane 3's agent is "selected." Scroll-sync and selection-highlight are deliberately separate concerns.

## Key constraints (acceptance criteria worth flagging)
- Count clamped to **1–10**; default conservative (2).
- **Same agent process/session is reused** — switching tiled views must *not respawn* agents.
- **Exiting tiled Dispatch must not kill agents** — returns to normal workspace.
- Needs horizontal overflow / responsive compression for high tile counts.

## Open questions still unresolved
- Persist across app reloads, or transient view mode?
- Should each lane remember its agent by session id across exits?
- Resizable lane widths? Pinned/sticky full-index lane while right lanes scroll horizontally?
- Preserve lane selections when tile count changes?

In short: it turns Dispatch from a one-agent-at-a-time command center into a **tiled, multi-lane cockpit** — one rich master index on the left, plus N independently-controllable live agent panes, with scroll-context sync that doesn't clobber per-lane selection. It directly serves the project's "run 5+ agents at once" thesis.

Note: this is the only issue about viewing multiple Dispatch lanes at once. (#236 and #261 are related Dispatch *bugs* — focus-stealing and focus-on-close — but #248 is the multi-lane feature itself.)

1	# Agent Code
2	
3	Agent Code is an agent-first editor for heavy users of Claude Code and Codex.
4	
5	This is not another "make Claude Code look nicer" wrapper. It is an
6	agentic development platform built on the opposite assumption: the agent
7	runtime is the product. The UI exists to make Claude Code and Codex more
8	powerful, not to replace them with a thin chat shell and a coat of glass.
9	
10	## Why This Exists
11	
12	A lot of people are building their own UI for Claude Code right now. Most
13	of them hit the same two failure modes:
14	
15	1. They optimize for surface aesthetics instead of agent capability.
16	2. They bypass the real product by driving unofficial or reduced flows that
17	   throw away the logic Claude Code and Codex already have.
18	
19	That leads to tools that look polished but are materially weaker.
20	
21	Agent Code takes a harder line:
22	
23	- Claude Code should still feel like Claude Code.
24	- Codex should still feel like Codex.
25	- The full command surface, prompts, tools, flows, and runtime behavior
26	  should still exist.
27	- The UI should add power for serious users, not abstract away the thing
28	  that already works.
29	
30	## Core Thesis
31	
32	The best agent editor is not a fake Claude Code UI.
33	
34	The best agent editor is a platform that runs the real Claude Code and the
35	real Codex under the hood, preserves their behavior, and then layers better
36	workspace primitives on top for people who spend all day in agent loops.
37	
38	That means Agent Code is built for:
39	
40	- parallel agent work
41	- persistent sessions
42	- richer workspace orchestration
43	- multi-pane and multi-provider flows
44	- better tooling around transcripts, state, terminals, and code context
45	
46	## Not OAuth Token Abuse
47	
48	Many wrappers depend on reusing OAuth tokens from Claude or Codex and then
49	calling private or reduced interfaces around the actual product.
50	
51	That approach is bad on two fronts:
52	
53	- It cuts against platform policy.
54	- It throws away an enormous amount of product logic that already exists in
55	  Claude Code and Codex.
56	
57	If you strip things down to "send message, get message back", you lose most
58	of what makes those tools good in practice.
59	
60	Agent Code is explicitly trying not to do that.
61	
62	## How It Works
63	
64	Agent Code runs Claude Code and Codex headlessly under the hood.
65	
66	But "headless" here does **not** mean using a minimal session API and
67	pretending that is the product.
68	
69	It means using open source headless runtimes that emulate the actual CLI and
70	terminal behavior of Claude Code and Codex so the shell can expose the full
71	system programmatically.
72	
73	The architecture combines:
74	
75	- terminal emulation
76	- JSON/event parsing
77	- screen parsing
78	- transcript parsing
79	- session management
80	
81	This lets Agent Code surface the real commands, flows, and tools from Claude
82	Code and Codex in an API-like way without collapsing them into a toy chat
83	interface.
84

86	
87	- `claude-code-headless`: headless control layer for Claude Code
88	- `codex-headless`: headless control layer for Codex
89	- `agent-transcript-parser`: translation layer between transcript formats
90	- Electron + React workspace shell on top
91	
92	## What This Project Is
93	
94	Agent Code is:
95	
96	- an Electron desktop shell for agent-heavy development
97	- a multi-session workspace for Claude Code, Codex, and terminals
98	- a way to preserve nearly all of the real agent behavior while adding a
99	  stronger editor and workspace model around it
100	
101	It is not:
102	
103	- a "Claude Code but prettier" theme project
104	- a thin chat app with editor chrome
105	- a wrapper that replaces the underlying product with a reduced API
106	
107	## Philosophy
108	
109	The job is not to "macify" Claude Code.
110	
111	The job is to build the editor serious agent users actually need:
112	
113	- keep the underlying agents real
114	- preserve the capabilities that already exist
115	- expose more control, more observability, and more workspace power
116	- build for people who live in long-running, high-volume agent sessions
117	
118	If the result ever looks nicer, that is incidental. Capability comes first.
119

124	
125	- Claude Code sessions
126	- Codex sessions
127	- plain terminal sessions
128	- tabbed and tiled workspace UI
129	- provider-aware session handling
130	- transcript and runtime parsing

4	
5	## Why build this?
6	
7	OpenCode is amazing. Cursor is amazing. The issue with these is that their software models are facing a hard time. Because of one reason:
8	
9	OAuth is being killed.
10	
11	You can no longer use Anthropic models properly in OpenCode, and Cursor's pricing is getting more brutal by the day if you do not lock yourself into their internal models.
12	
13	But everybody wants to use SOTA models, which basically means Claude's latest and Codex's latest releases. Codex is liberal with OAuth usage as of me writing this, but my prediction is that that will not last forever. This is history repeating itself; in the 2010s the definition of the internet was "open." Everybody had free APIs to access their whole software suite. Facebook, Google, Yahoo, etc. This just slowly got killed by the companies. The difference is that, as with everything in AI, it is compressing the internet's timeline into 5 years instead of 20, and we already saw Anthropic banning OAuth.
14	
15	## What Agent Code does differently
16	
17	Instead of trying to go around Claude Code and Codex, it is just the middleman. When you use the app, a headless CLI for Claude and Codex is spawned. Do not confuse this with the SDK that is natively exposed, because that is limited and drops 75% of the functionality that lives in Codex and Claude. What Agent Code runs in a PTY is the FULL native Claude Code and Codex. This allows us to keep and maintain all new and custom functionality that these providers expose.
18	
19	## So why do this?
20	
21	Building an app like this lets me add any abstractions that I want, but the main motivations behind it were the following:
22	
23	**1. Provider switching.**
24	I built a package that Agent Code calls for this sole purpose: [agent-transcript-parser](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-transcript-parser). This allows you to have a Codex session open, open the command palette and switch to Claude in one click, by natively translating the JSONL transcript between the two providers.
25	
26	**2. Heavy development focus.**
27	This might be the most important part. Codex and Claude's apps focus on having one session on the screen and feel like they are built for lightweight agent development. Using agents properly requires having 5 running at all times. Agent Code gives you excellent tiling built in to manage all of your agents in a grid structure.
28	
29	**3. Custom rendering.**
30	Because we are positioning Agent Code as a middleman, we rewrite all the rendering in React. This allows us to do whatever we want. For example, we built a better UI to see what the agents committed and ran for git commands.
31	
32	**4. Opinionated for efficiency.**
33	The whole app is built for efficient development. All terminals are tmux-persistent by default alongside all agents. There are 50+ commands which are all excellent to boost productivity on top of the agents.
34	
35	## Structure
36	
37	One of the principles I understood early is that getting open-source contributors on board with something like this is hard. So Agent Code is dependent on 4 separate projects that it imports as packages, all more broadly scoped, which will hopefully attract more open-source attention.
38	
39	## Structure
40	
41	One of the principles I understood early is that getting open-source contributors on board with something like this is hard. So Agent Code is dependent on 4 separate projects that it imports as packages — all more broadly scoped, which will hopefully attract more open-source attention.
42	
43	**1. Headless Claude Code and Codex**
44	[claude-code-headless](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/claude-code-headless) · [codex-headless](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/codex-headless)
45	This is basically the core of the app. It takes the full Claude CLI and Codex CLI and exposes them as an API, so that you can control all actions that you would be able to do in the CLI programmatically instead. For example, detecting the state when the agent is running a compaction or when the agent is asking for folder permission. You could take this and make it the backend of any project you want.
46	
47	**2. [Agent Transcript Parser](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-transcript-parser)**
48	As mentioned before — takes a JSONL transcript from Codex and converts it to Claude or vice versa with complete roundtrip safety.
49	
50	**3. [Agent Voice Dictation](https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-voice-dictation)**
51	This is a clone of WhisprFlow that is fully open-source but built on Deepgram, which allows you to get $200 in free credits that will last you a lifetime. The repo does ship an Electron app if you prefer to consume it that way, but also a client that Agent Code relies on so that all agent inputs can ship voice dictation natively.
52	
53	Worth mentioning that Agent Code is opinionated with cleverness over the whole suite. For instance: WhisprFlow is stupid — they are trying to correct spelling mistakes on the wrong level. They are trying to make their AI correct the mistakes before passing it into the model. It is the model that has all the context; the model can do the correction itself. So in Agent Code the simple solution is just wrapping the voice dictation in a custom tag explaining to Claude Code or Codex that the prompt may contain obvious mistakes:
54	
55	```xml
56	<stt note="Speech-to-text; may contain transcription mistakes.">
57	Now I am speaking.
58	</stt>
59	```

1	# Reporting Issues
2	
3	This codebase is worked on primarily by AI agents. This guide is for
4	them.
5	
6	**The more technical detail, the better.** File paths with line numbers,
7	exact symbols, transcript IDs, commit SHAs, error output verbatim,
8	stack traces, environment variables — over-share rather than
9	under-share. Every fact you omit is a follow-up round trip the next
10	person has to do before they can reproduce.
11	
12	## Which repo
13	
14	| Repo | What goes here |
15	|---|---|
16	| **agent-code** | UI, tile-tree, dispatch, session management, IPC, system-perf, settings — all renderer + main-process behaviour. Default. |
17	| **claude-code-headless** | Driving the real `claude` CLI: TUI parsing, JSONL handling, proxy/SSE streaming, slash-picker, permission prompts. |
18	| **codex-headless** | Driving the real `codex` CLI: rollout parsing, Responses adapter, screen parsing, approval overlays. |
19	| **agent-transcript-parser** | Claude↔Codex transcript translation, ghost primitives, rewind/clone helpers. |
20	| **agent-voice-dictation** | Recording, STT clients, OpenRouter polish, composer integration. |
21	
22	## Bug report
23	
24	```markdown
25	### What happened
26	One or two sentences. The visible symptom.
27	
28	### Repro
29	Exact steps. If non-deterministic, say so explicitly and describe how
30	often / under what conditions: "happens after ~30 min of normal use
31	with 10+ agents active." Link the relevant transcript path —
32	`~/.claude/projects/-Users-foo-bar/<sessionId>.jsonl` for Claude or
33	`~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<timestamp>-<id>.jsonl` for
34	Codex. Include the commit SHA you reproduced on.
35	
36	### Where
37	File:line and the function or symbol if you've located it. Examples:
38	`src/main/sessionManager.ts:912 spawnClaude`,
39	`src/renderer/src/features/feed/ui/Feed.tsx onScroll`,
40	`packages/claude-code-headless/src/proxy/ClaudeProxyAdapter.ts:804`.
41	If unlocated, name the subsystem: feed renderer, JSONL tailer, proxy
42	adapter, dispatch mode, work-context, image paste, dictation.
43	
44	### Output
45	Error text, stack trace, log lines — verbatim, don't paraphrase or
46	truncate. Include surrounding console lines if a single line was the
47	trigger but the context is in the lines around it. Native frames
48	(C++/Rust) in a v8 fatal-error trace are important — keep them.
49	
50	### State
51	Anything that affects reproducibility: number of active panes, which
52	providers (Claude / Codex / terminal), how long the app had been
53	running, whether `AGENT_CODE_PERF` was set, whether you were in
54	Dispatch Mode, whether worktrees were attached.
55	```
56	
57	## Feature request
58	
59	```markdown
60	### Use case
61	The workflow the current app makes harder than it should be.
62	
63	### Example
64	One concrete scenario, end to end — what you'd do today vs. what you
65	wish you could do.
66	
67	### (Optional) Sketch
68	Implementation thoughts. Skip unless you have specifics.
69	```
70	
71	## Performance / crash
72	
73	Different evidence than functional bugs. Attach what applies:
74	
75	- **Fatal-error block from the terminal.** When the main process
76	  OOM's, the terminal where `npm start` ran will have a `FATAL
77	  ERROR: CALL_AND_RETRY_LAST Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out
78	  of memory` line followed by a `Native stack trace` block. Include
79	  the whole block, not just the headline — the native frames identify
80	  the allocator that broke (typical signatures: `node::Buffer::New`,
81	  `v8::CppHeap::wrapper_descriptor`, Rust `font_types::...`).
82	- **System-perf popover state at the time.** Requires
83	  `AGENT_CODE_PERF=1` set when launching. Click the heap badge in the
84	  header. Report: heap used / limit, RSS, top heap spaces with sizes
85	  (especially `old_space` and `large_object_space`),
86	  detached-contexts count, native-contexts count, event-loop p99,
87	  60s growth Δ for heap and RSS.
88	- **Heap snapshot.** Manual: click "Capture heap snapshot" in the
89	  popover; writes to `~/.config/agent-code/heap-snapshots/manual-<iso>-<pid>.heapsnapshot`.
90	  Automatic: the watchdog writes one when `used_heap_size` crosses
91	  `min(3 GiB, 0.75 × heap_size_limit)` — same directory, `main-` prefix.
92	  These files are 10–500 MB; link a cloud share rather than attaching
93	  directly if large.
94	- **Growth pattern.** Three shapes matter:
95	  - steady monotonic climb → retention leak
96	  - spike-up-then-drop-to-zero cycle → transient large allocations
97	    (whole-file reads, big buffers, GC churn)
98	  - sudden jump → one-shot allocation (giant string, image, file load)
99	
100	  Saying which shape you observed narrows the suspect list before
101	  anyone opens the snapshot.
102	
103	## Security
104	
105	Disclose privately to the maintainer rather than via a public GitHub
106	issue.
107	
108	## Don't file
109	
110	- How-to questions → Discussions.
111	- Upstream CLI bugs (`claude` / `codex` flag behaviour) → the upstream
112	  repos for those tools, not here.

1. They optimize for **looks** instead of agent capability ("Claude Code but prettier").
2. They **bypass the real product** — driving the limited SDK or reusing OAuth tokens against private/reduced interfaces, which throws away ~75% of the functionality that lives in the real CLIs.

Agent Code takes the opposite stance: **the agent runtime is the product; the UI exists to make it more powerful.** It runs the *full, real* `claude` and `codex` CLIs headlessly inside PTYs — not the stripped-down SDK — so the entire command surface, prompts, tools, permission flows, and runtime behavior are preserved. ## The strategic bet (from MANIFESTO.md)

The motivating insight: **OAuth is being killed.** You can no longer use Anthropic models properly in OpenCode, and Cursor's pricing punishes you for using SOTA external models. The prediction is that the "open API" era of AI tools will close fast (history rhyming with how Facebook/Google/Yahoo killed their open APIs in the 2010s, but compressed into ~5 years). So instead of going *around* Claude Code and Codex, Agent Code becomes **the middleman** that drives them natively.

## How it works architecturally

A headless CLI for Claude/Codex is spawned in a PTY and controlled programmatically. The stack combines terminal emulation, JSON/event parsing, screen parsing, transcript parsing, and session management — exposing the real CLIs in an API-like way. On top sits an **Electron + React workspace shell**.

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| **claude-code-headless** | Drives the real `claude` CLI — TUI parsing, JSONL handling, proxy/SSE streaming, slash-picker, permission prompts |
| **codex-headless** | Drives the real `codex` CLI — rollout parsing, Responses adapter, screen parsing, approval overlays |
| **opencode-headless** | (additional headless control layer) |
| **agent-transcript-parser** | Translates JSONL transcripts between Claude ↔ Codex with roundtrip safety — this is what powers **one-click provider switching** mid-session |
| **agent-voice-dictation** | Open-source WhisprFlow clone on Deepgram; ships voice dictation natively into the composer (wraps STT output in an `<stt>` tag so the *model* fixes transcription errors, not a dumb pre-pass) |

- **`src/shared/`** — git, parsers, runtime, types, work-context, rendered-content

- Testing recently moved to **Vitest** (commit #263), with unit / integration / renderer projects.

Active build. Recent commit activity is heavily focused on the **feed rendering rewrite** and **orchestration** (multi-agent context inheritance, handoff scanning) — there are active rewrite plans in `docs/rendering/` and `docs/codex-rewrite-render/`.

---

# Tiled Dispatch

## Summary

Add a `Tiled Dispatch` command that lets the user enter a tile count, up to 10, and opens a multi-lane Dispatch layout where several live agents can be viewed and controlled at the same time.

## Problem

Dispatch Mode is useful for managing many agents, but it currently behaves like a single command-center surface. That means the user can see the list of agents, pick one, and work with that agent, but they cannot easily keep multiple active agents visible side by side from the Dispatch workflow.

When coordinating several Claude/Codex agents, the user often wants both:

- A full Dispatch index with all worktrees, section titles, agent types, and full agent titles.
- Multiple live agent views on screen at once, each with a small local selector for switching that lane to another agent.

The existing single Dispatch surface makes that workflow too serial.

## Proposed Behavior

Add a command:

```text
Tiled Dispatch
```

When run, the command prompts the user for a number:

```text
How many dispatch tiles? 1-10
```

After the user enters `N`, Agent Code enters a tiled Dispatch layout:

```text
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ DISPATCH INDEX       │ AGENT VIEW 1                 │ MINI LIST  │ AGENT VIEW 2                 │ MINI LIST  │ AGENT VIEW 3                 │
│ full list            │ selected agent               │ compact    │ selected agent               │ compact    │ selected agent               │
│                      │                              │            │                              │            │                              │
│ Worktree: app        │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ ● Agent A  │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ ● Agent B  │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
│  Claude  Agent A  ◀  │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │ ● Agent B◀ │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │ ● Agent C◀ │ │ Claude/Codex transcript  │ │
│  Codex   Agent B     │ │ composer / terminal      │ │ ● Agent C  │ │ composer / terminal      │ │ ● Agent D  │ │ composer / terminal      │ │
│  Claude  Agent C     │ │ live output              │ │ ● Agent D  │ │ live output              │ │ ● Agent E  │ │ live output              │ │
│                      │ │                          │ │            │ │                          │ │            │ │                          │ │
│ Worktree: issue-211  │ │ selected from index      │ │ no groups  │ │ selected from mini list  │ │ no groups  │ │ selected from mini list  │ │
│  Codex   Agent D     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │ no cwd     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │ no cwd     │ └──────────────────────────┘ │
│  Claude  Agent E     │                              │ no type    │                              │ no type    │                              │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
```

For `N` tiled lanes, the conceptual layout is:

```text
[full dispatch index] [agent view 1] [mini list 2] [agent view 2] ... [mini list N] [agent view N]
```

The first lane is special:

- It keeps the full Dispatch list UI.
- It shows full section titles.
- It shows worktree/project grouping.
- It shows agent type/provider labels.
- It acts as the global index for the whole tiled Dispatch layout.

Every later lane uses a compact local selector:

- It shows a minimal agent list.
- It omits repeated section titles.
- It omits repeated worktree labels.
- It omits repeated agent type/provider labels.
- It is only there to switch which agent is shown in that lane.

Each lane still has a real live agent view beside its list. This is not just multiple copies of the Dispatch list; the point is to make multiple agents visible and usable at the same time.

## Scroll and Selection Sync

When the user scrolls a compact mini list, the full Dispatch index on the far left should follow that scroll position enough to keep the same region of the agent list/context visible. The full index remains the source of truth for rich context: section titles, worktrees, provider labels, and full agent titles.

Selection highlighting is separate from scroll sync:

- The full index still highlights the agent selected in lane 1.
- A compact mini list highlights the agent selected for its own lane.
- Scrolling mini list 3 should move the full index to the same approximate list region, but it should not make the full index pretend that lane 3's agent is selected.
- This lets the user use the full left index as context while still seeing exactly which agent belongs to lane 1.

In other words:

```text
Lane 3 mini list scrolls
        │
        ▼
Full left index follows scroll/context
        │
        └── but selected highlight remains Agent 1 / lane 1
```

## UX Notes

- The default tile count should be conservative, probably `2` or the previous value if one exists.
- The max should be clamped to `10`.
- The layout needs horizontal overflow or responsive compression for high tile counts.
- The first/full Dispatch index should stay readable even when there are many lanes.
- Compact mini lists should be dense and stable, optimized for quick lane switching.
- The selected agent per lane should be independent.
- Switching one lane should not steal focus or selection from the other lanes.
- Scrolling a compact mini list should sync the full index's scroll context, while preserving the full index's own selected-agent highlight.

## Open Questions

- Should tiled Dispatch persist across app reloads, or should it be a transient Dispatch view mode?
- Should each lane remember its selected agent by session id across normal Dispatch exits/reentries?
- Should lane widths be resizable?
- Should the full index lane be pinned/sticky while the right-side lanes horizontally scroll?
- Should tile count changes preserve current lane selections where possible?

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `Tiled Dispatch` command exists.
- Running it prompts for a tile count from `1` to `10`.
- Entering a valid count opens a tiled Dispatch layout.
- The leftmost lane shows the full Dispatch index with section titles, worktree grouping, provider/agent type labels, and full titles.
- Each additional lane shows a compact mini list plus the actual selected agent view to its right.
- Each lane can select a different live agent.
- Scrolling a compact mini list scroll-syncs the full left Dispatch index to the same general list region.
- The full left Dispatch index continues to highlight lane 1's selected agent, even while its scroll position follows another lane's mini list.
- The same agent process/session is reused; switching tiled views must not respawn agents.
- Exiting tiled Dispatch returns the user to the normal workspace without killing agents.
- Invalid counts are rejected or clamped safely.

## The problem it solves
Dispatch Mode today is a **single command-center surface**: you see the list of all your agents, pick *one*, and work with it. That's serial. When you're coordinating 5+ Claude/Codex agents, you want two things at once that the current design can't give you:

1. A **full index** of every agent (worktrees, section titles, provider labels, full titles).
2. **Several live agent views side-by-side**, each independently switchable.

- Each lane shows a *different live agent*, and they're independent — switching one lane doesn't steal focus or selection from another.

## The clever bit — scroll vs. selection decoupling
This is the subtle design point. When you scroll a mini-list (say lane 3), the **full left index follows that scroll position** so you keep rich context for the region you're browsing — **but the left index's *highlight* stays on lane 1's selected agent.** So scrolling lane 3 moves the index's viewport without making it pretend lane 3's agent is "selected." - Needs horizontal overflow / responsive compression for high tile counts.

- Persist across app reloads, or transient view mode?
- Should each lane remember its agent by session id across exits?
- Resizable lane widths? Pinned/sticky full-index lane while right lanes scroll horizontally?
- Preserve lane selections when tile count changes?
